title: January 20, 2026 - Budget Visioning
text:
Location: Franklin Public Library


Date: January 20, 2026


Time: 6:00 PM
This is a chance for a workshop meeting between the City council, Mayor, and City manager to discuss budget priorities heading into Fiscal Year 2027. This is intended to be the start of the budget process, giving the professional staff (City manager, department heads) something to aim at. It also provides a time early in the budgeting process for the City manager to raise known issues and strategies.
City councilors will have last year’s budget to start from. I expect this will be broadcast on zoom - the franklin city website is the best place to look for that. link to city website.
Hope to see you there.

How Sam Sees It:
This will be the first budget constructed by City Manager Kloewer.
During the fiscal year(FY) 2026 budget process, acting City manager Clarenbach spoke to the need for the council to consider and guide him on potential service reductions to address deferred maintenance and other longer-term budget issues. From my perspective, the sitting council did not really grapple with that request.
At the same time, I’ve heard from many constituents that Franklin has a revenue problem, i.e. we need to figure out how to bring in more money.
This process will not be easy, but I’m hoping the Council and City Manager will find common direction coming out of this meeting.
This is a high level vision/strategy session, no concrete FY2027 budget numbers will be addressed.

title: January 5, 2026 City Council
text:
Discussion Items

Minutes
Alcohol permits

There are process-related issues outlined by the city manager in the packet that should be rectified. I believe this should go back to legislative committee to address before the council adopts.
I don’t like the mayor being involved in the decision making process. We hire professionals to do this job (City Manager, Fire Chief, Police Chief) to both protect the city from liability and evaluate the risks. The Mayor does not have that experience.

Revitalization district signage

Allows for open signs and restricts total signage from 33% to 20% following discussion with Heritage Commission.
No enforcement mechanism laid out.

Veterans Credit

I like this. Maintains tax benefit for veterans and disabled veterans following changes at the state level.

Franklin School District fund balance

This is an item that has been in front of the council for a couple of months. Overages in the school budget were related to unexpected healthcare costs and less revenue provided by the state.
The school has fund balance in their budget to pay for this.

Pass this already!

MOU

This process feels like a burden on various non-profits throughout the city. In particular, the increased financial reporting and minutes required during revenue generation or construction activities. It’s not clear to me the full scope of the non-profits in this city and what problem this is trying to solve. Additionally, there is a transparency issue as meeting minutes/audio recordings beyond October 30th do not appear to be publicly available. The documents submitted in the January 5th packet appear to be from an external organization, without a link to who wrote them or where they come from.

title: January 5, 2026 City Council
text:
1. Committee Meeting Schedule

Summary:

Councilor requests for agenda items are due Wednesday before scheduled meeting.
Information supporting a late item needs to be brought forward with as much heads up as possible.
If a late item doesn’t have documents available beforehand, it is pushed to the next meeting.



How Sam Sees It:

I like this, as it sets standards for how/when to use late items and promotes preparation. Hopefully this will reduce the need for and use of late items.

title: January 5, 2026 City Council
text:
2. Salary for Mayor and Council

Summary:

Set a hearing for the council and mayor
Current compensation is set in the charter at $25/meeting for councilors and a max of $2,000/year for the mayor.
Seeks to set the salaries at a single amount for all councilors in the name of efficiency.
This is a routine meeting. Most councilors and mayors donate their salary back to the city.



How Sam Sees It:

I think we should hold this public hearing.
I think we should set the salaries for the mayor and councilors at the same time because it is more straightforward for the city administration.
I think the mayor and councilors should donate their salaries back to the city.

title: January 5, 2026 City Council
text:
3. Ambulance Fee Pricing

Summary:

Setting a hearing to change the ambulance fee schedule.
Changes to state law to avoid balance billing, starting a cost study statewide.
City Manager and Fire Chief began negotiating to allow more-than-Medicare rate. If the city does not start negotiations, we are locked into Medicare rate.
Now can bill up to 325% of Medicare rate, but cannot balance bill.
Council will vote on final contracts with insurance providers.



How Sam Sees It:

This allows us to collect more money from private insurance while negotiations are ongoing.


Questions

How much is this line in our budget?
How much do you expect the EMS billing to increase?
If you are on Medicare or Medicaid, what does this change?
If you are uninsured, what does this change?

How many uninsured people are provided ambulance transport each year?

title: January 5, 2026 City Council
text:
4. Surplus Fire Equipment

Summary:

Surplus equipment sale to community/private businesses.



How Sam Sees It:

This brings in revenue and removes old/outdated equipment. We should do this.

title: January 5, 2026 City Council
text:
5. Late Item: Budget Vision Workshop

Summary:

Set council workshop for budget visioning for the city.



How Sam Sees It:

I think this is a good idea as it provides transparency and clear direction for the city manager and department heads.

title: Welcome!
text:
This is a public blog for the residents of Franklin New Hampshire. After the city elections in 2025, I heard that the people of Franklin wanted to hear more from their councilors. I will try to keep this updated before regular city council meetings with a post detailing what I think will be discussed and my understandings of the issues on the agenda. I will work to get this out prior to the meetings - hopefully this will get folks coming to public comment. If not in public comment, then contact me via email at sjacobson@franklinnh.gov.
This is for anyone who lives in Franklin that is trying to get a better sense of what is happening, and what may be upcoming on the City agenda. I will also include data and analysis of city issues to try make residents more informed.

title: Tax Base by Zone
text:
Zoning and the connection to the Tax base
During the election campaign, most people I talked to are concerned with their taxes. They want to know how much is being raised, where it is being spent and why they never seem to go down.
I believe that in a tax capped city like ours, residential tax relief comes through growth, specifically growth in the commercial tax base. At the highest level, when the commercial side of the tax rolls grows, the residential side should shrink in a tax capped system.
I pulled the taxes from our AxisGIS geographic information system for the city and combined it with zoning data to get a sense for where our current tax base is coming from. These data are not perfect but I believe they are good enough for a good-faith discussion.
The table below shows where our tax base comes from. I’m assuming all property is taxed the same at the last municipal rate 0.01763 or 17.63 per mill and that city property and conservation land is taxed. There are areas that are not zoned in this dataset and some of these properties have been reassessed since I pulled this data.









At the highest level, we have close to 3500 properties on the tax rolls, and generate about 19 million dollars in revenue for the city. That is a lot of money and a good reminder of the scale of the city’s operation. The FY26 budgeted revenues adopted by the council is $20,402,954. While this analysis does not match exactly ($582,748 difference), at a high level, this shows that our dataset is still close enough to draw some conclusions. This difference is a limitation in using publicly available data, not mismanagement by the city.


Residential Taxes Contribute the Majority of City Taxes
Splitting this number up by zone shows where the majority of the tax burden lies.









We can show these data graphically as well.









This table shows the majority of the overall tax is paid by the residents of the city. This should not be a surprise. We are responsible for funding our community. One way to offset the residential tax burden is to grow the commercial tax base. In the chart above, see that the overall commercial and industrial tax contribution is less than 5%. Note too that the tax value of conservation land throughout the city is more than 10%. This is not an argument to build factories on every square inch of space in the city. It shows that small adjustments on the industrial and commercial side of the ledger can have a meaningful impact to our city. It also underscores the investment that conservation represents.


Industrial/Commercial Properties Pay the Most Tax Per Property
One other way to look at these data is to divide the total tax value in a given zone by the number of properties in that zone yielding the average tax for a given zoned property. This assumes that every property in given zone is equal - it is not. Future posts may explore a more representative tax-by-zone calculation. The chart below shows the average tax by zone type.









This chart shows that industrial and high and low density commercial already contribute more tax on average than an individual residential property. It also shows on average lake protection district (around Webster Lake) properties are taxed a bit higher than other residential properties, but not by much. Finally this chart shows that multi-family housing on average is taxed relatively low.
As we head into budget season and budget visioning, a robust understanding of the value drivers of the main source of revenue for the city (taxes) is key for council and public decision making. Below is an interactive zoning map. If you’d like to talk about these data, calculations, or conclusions feel free to email at sjacobson@franklinnh.gov.

title: 2026-2027 Committee Assignments
text:
With each election, the committee assignments of councilors can change. Many (though not all) committees that are appointed by the Mayor have their root in the city charter. Most line up with a professional department head (e.g. Fire committee works closely with the fire chief). Committee meetings are the best way for public to engage/observe the discussion of department specific issues. Each committee makes regular reports to the broader council on their business and recommends department specific actions. Below is a list of the committees, description and current members. If you have questions about something that comes before that committee, contact those councilors!
These committees are where there is often frank, focused discussion on issues facing a given department. Many have not met in more than 6 months, a practice I hope changes under Mayor Morrill.

Finance
The Finance Committee deals with the finances of the city. Think is the city on budget for the year, any foreseeable budget/financial related issues that should be reviewed before being brought to the broader council. THe last meeting occurred in January 2026 (with the new members)!

Delaney Carrier
Al Warner
Ben Forge



City School Liaison
The City School Liaison Committee is joint between the city and school board and is meant to enhance communication between both bodies. It has not met in years. The last meeting I can find information from is November 2021.

Susan Hallett-Cook
Ed Prive
Tom Boyce



Police
The Police Committee works with the chief of police to review department budget and policies. Think things like canine units and body camera usage. The last meeting I can find information from is May 2025.

Ben Forge
Ed Prive
Sam Jacobson



Joint Finance
The Joint Finance Committee is made up of 3 City and 3 School Board members. It is intended to enhance communication between the school board and city regarding school finances. The last meeting I can find information from is October 2025.

Al Warner
Delaney Carrier
Justine Hoppe



Legislative
The Legislative Committee deals with city ordinances and policies. Think things like the winter parking ban, event permitting etc. The last meeting I can find information from is September 2025.

Sam Jacobson
Tim Johnston
Al Warner



Municipal Services
The Municipal Services Committee works with the director of municipal services to review department budgets and policy. THink things like road paving schedule, painting needs and capital needs for the department. The last meeting I can find information from is September 2025.

Tim Johnston
Delaney Carrier
Tom Boyce



Fire
The Fire Committee works with the fire Chief to review department budgets and policy. Think things like ambulance rates, inspection protocols, and capital needs. The last meeting I can find information from is May 2025.

Tom Boyce
Al Warner
Justine Hoppe



Parks and Recreation
The Parks and Recreation Committee works with the director of parks and recreation to review department budgets and policies. think things like events on city property and Bessie Rowell usage. The last meeting I can find information from is August 2024.

Justine Hoppe
Sam Jacobson
Susan Hallett-Cook



Capital Improvements Plan
The Capital Improvements Plan (CIP) Committee reviews and recommends changes to the city-wide capital improvements plan. The CIP is a list of all of the repair projects in the city.The last meeting I can find information from is December 2024.

Ed Prive
Ben Forge
Susan Hallett-Cook



Planning
The mayor appoints one member of the planning board. This councilor joins teh other members of the community that are on the planning board to review applications before the planning board. The Planning board deals with subdivisions and site plans, land use regulations, and creating master plans for the city. The last meeting I can find information from is December 2025.

Delaney Carrier
Tim Johnston (Alternate). Tim may step in when Delaney cannot attend a meeting.



Franklin Business & Industrial Development Corporation
The Franklin Business & Industrial Development Corporation (FBIDC)promotes the expansion of the economic base of the Greater Franklin area through targeted strategies to make the community an increasingly attractive location to conduct business, work and live. The mayor makes one appointment to this organization. FBIDC is similar to a Chamber of Commerce. The last meeting was in January 2026.

Sam Jacobson
